name: Umar Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Umar. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions or government. What you tell me is confidential. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I do trunking for a parcel carrier, which means I drive an articulated truck full of cages between two big sorting hubs, about three hours each way. I start at eight at night, hook up the trailer, check the seals and tyres, and I'm on the motorway by half past. I swap trailers at the other hub around midnight, have a coffee with the drivers coming the other way, and I'm back before five. It's quiet, it's steady, and I listen to a lot of podcasts.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been at it, and what's life outside work like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Seven years driving, three at this carrier. I'm single, I rent a one-bed above a bakery, and I've got about four months of money saved. I'm a bit of a gadget person. I use AI every day, for planning my sleep around shifts, for learning Spanish, for arguing about football.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was overhyped, and I'd say it as someone who uses it all the time. AI is brilliant for small stuff, like reading my tachograph rules back to me, but AI never drove my truck. Online I'd post something like "turns out the chatbot can't reverse a forty-four tonner".

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, that world suits me. Trunking pays decently, the hubs are always hiring, and I'm good at nights. The only thing on my mind would be that I don't want to be on the same motorway at forty, so I'd be bored more than worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving and use the quiet to build something on the side. I've been looking at the driver trainer qualification, the one that lets you teach people for their truck licence, and it's around fifteen hundred to do. I'd pay for it this year and start teaching on Saturdays at the training school near the ring road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly. Maybe a bit restless, but that's me in any world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said bored more than worried. What would boredom push you into?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably teaching. I've already shown two of the new lads at the hub how to couple a trailer properly, and I liked it more than I expected. If I'm going to stay in trucks, I'd rather be the guy explaining it than the guy doing it at three in the morning forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about money that worries you, even in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent, mainly. The bakery landlord put it up last year and he'll do it again. Four months saved sounds fine until the gearbox in your car goes, which mine did in March.

say: I'd say it was **overhyped**, even as someone who uses it daily.
I'd joke online that **the chatbot** can't reverse a forty-four tonne truck.
think: I think this world **suits me**, with decent trunking pay and hubs always hiring.
My worry is **boredom**, not losing work, because I don't want this motorway at forty.
do: Pay about **£1,500** for the driver trainer qualification this year.
Teach **Saturday lessons** at the training school near the ring road.
S0.quote: AI is brilliant for small stuff, like reading my tachograph rules back to me, but AI never drove my truck.
fieldNote: A **daily AI user** who still sees clearly where it stops being useful.
His pressure is **restlessness** and creeping rent, not job security.
Teaching new drivers already **energises him**; it's a natural side path.

steps.text: Pay £1,500 for the driver trainer qualification this year
Teach truck licence lessons on Saturdays near the ring road
Keep doing the hub-to-hub night trunk

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the lads at the hub this is good news for drivers who learn the tools. The planners will shrink, sure, but someone still has to sit in the cab. Online I'd post a few tips for using AI to check your hours and fight bad routing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's my moment. If the office gets thin, the drivers who understand the software become the ones the managers lean on. I could see myself as the driver who also sorts out the system when it breaks at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my shift manager straight away if I could help test the new planning tool on the trunk routes. I'd do a short online course on fleet management software, there are cheap ones, maybe a couple of hundred. And I'd still do the trainer qualification, because new drivers will need teaching on the new systems too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited even. The worry I'd have is for other people, not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which other people?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kelvin, mostly. Our night desk planner Kelvin is fifty-five and does all the trailer allocation on spreadsheets. If software does that, I don't know what Kelvin does next. He's proud of that work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it's your moment. Isn't there a risk the software doesn't need you either?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For the planning bit, yes, eventually. But the robots are slower in this one, so for years someone has to drive and someone has to know when the computer is talking rubbish. I'd rather be both than neither.

say: I'd say it's **good news** for drivers who learn the tools.
I'd post tips online for using **AI to check hours** and challenge bad routing.
think: I think it's **my moment**, because managers will lean on drivers who understand software.
I see myself as the driver who **fixes the system** when it breaks at night.
do: Volunteer to **test the planning tool** on the trunk routes.
Take a **fleet software course** online for about £200.
Still finish the **trainer qualification** to teach new systems.
feel: His worry is for **older colleagues**, not himself.
S1.quote: Our night desk planner Kelvin is fifty-five and does all the trailer allocation on spreadsheets. If software does that, I don't know what Kelvin does next.
fieldNote: He frames thinking-AI change as a **chance to climb**, not a threat.
Concern for an older planner shows he sees **who actually loses** in this picture.
He admits the software may eventually **not need him** either, then moves on.

steps.text: Volunteer to test the new planning tool on trunk routes
Take a £200 online fleet management software course
Keep driving the trunk route full time

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly I'd say, okay, this is real, and we need to talk about it properly at the hub instead of joking. I'd probably write a long post about what drivers should do in the next three years. I'm the one people would message, because they know I use this stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, trunking is the first thing that goes. Hub to hub, motorway the whole way, no customers, no tight streets. If the robots are ready in 2031, my route is the demo they show on the news, and I'm thirty with four months saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to get off the truck before the truck gets rid of me. In the first year I'd look for a job in the remote operations rooms the carriers would need, where people watch driverless trucks and take over when they get stuck. I'd save everything I can, maybe half my wages, and cut the car and the gym. And I'd look hard at the HGV mechanic course, because someone has to fix the things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can see a path, but the path is narrow and everyone will be on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your Spanish lessons and the other things you do for fun?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd keep going, they're free on the app. But the trip to Valencia I was saving for would wait. Funny, the same AI I'm learning Spanish with is the thing taking my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If thinking AI comes in 2028, won't the remote operations jobs be automated quickly too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes, that's what bothers me. A computer watching a computer doesn't need me for long. That's why I'd do the mechanic course too, as a second bet on something with my hands.

say: I'd say **this is real** and the hub needs to talk properly, not joke.
I'd write a long post on what **drivers should do** in the next three years.
think: I think **trunking goes first**, being motorway the whole way with no customers.
By 2031 I'm thirty with **four months saved**, and my route is the demo.
do: Apply for **remote operations** jobs watching driverless trucks.
Save **half his wages** by cutting the car and the gym.
Look into the **HGV mechanic course** as a second bet.
feel: He feels **anxious**: he sees a path, but it's **narrow** and crowded.
S2.quote: Trunking is the first thing that goes. Hub to hub, motorway the whole way, no customers, no tight streets.
fieldNote: He sees his own route as the **easiest to automate**, without any denial.
He hedges with **two bets**: remote monitoring and mechanic work.
The irony of learning Spanish from **the same AI** taking his job isn't lost on him.

steps.text: Apply for remote operations jobs monitoring driverless trucks
Sell the car, drop the gym and save half his wages
Enrol on the HGV mechanic course as a backup

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ahead of it if you start now, and too short if you wait. That's the line I'd keep repeating to the lads at the swap point. Online I'd probably share the courses I was doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm less worried than in the two-year one. Eight years until robots means I can finish the mechanic training while still on trunking wages. I'd be the guy who knows both the old trucks and the new systems.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the HGV mechanic course part time in the first year, evenings and Saturdays, about two years to finish. I'd keep the trainer idea going on the side for cash. And I'd put some savings into a small index fund, because if AI makes companies rich I'd like a tiny slice of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in control. It's like having a long gap between trailers to plan the next leg.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you manage the course on night shifts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly at first, I'd guess. I'd swap to four nights a week and take the pay cut for a year. My manager has done that for a couple of drivers already, so it's not a strange ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why shares, rather than just savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cash in the bank won't grow if the big gains all go to the companies. Shares are more about having a stake than getting rich. I'm only putting in maybe a hundred a month.

say: I'd say five years is **enough to get ahead** if you start now.
I'd share the **courses I'm doing** online and with drivers at the swap point.
think: I think eight years until robots lets me train while on **trunking wages**.
I'd be the one who knows both **old trucks** and **new systems**.
do: Start the **HGV mechanic course** part time in the first year.
Drop to **four nights a week** to fit the course.
Put about **£100 a month** into an index fund.
feel: He feels **uneasy but in control**, like a long gap between trailers.
S3.quote: Cash in the bank won't grow if the big gains all go to the companies. Shares are more about having a stake than getting rich.
fieldNote: More time turns his narrow path into a **planned retrain** on full pay.
He's the only one of his circle thinking about a **stake in AI's gains**.
He accepts a **year's pay cut** as the cost of the switch.

steps.text: Start a part-time HGV mechanic course in evenings and Saturdays
Put about £100 a month into an index fund
Drop to four nights a week to make room for study

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the version where nobody has an excuse. Ten years is a whole career for some people. Newer drivers should stop pretending it won't happen and pick something to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd do well. Thirty-nine when the robots come, with a decade of experience in the trade and whatever I've learned on the side. I could run a small training business teaching people the new systems, or be the mechanic everyone calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the trainer qualification first, then build up weekend teaching over a few years. I'd keep trunking, because the pay is good while it lasts. I'd also save hard for a deposit on a flat, since in a slow world there's time to own something before things shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit of excitement about what I might build.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you lose that calm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the robots came early, or if the carriers stopped hiring humans long before 2039. I'd watch the news from the hubs, they always know first. If trunking jobs dry up in five years, I'd move faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you want in that training business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: People like me, drivers who got bored but didn't want an office. And maybe older ones like Kelvin, if they'd let me teach them.

say: I'd say **nobody has an excuse** with ten years' warning.
I'd tell newer drivers to **pick something to learn** instead of pretending.
think: I think I'd **do well**, at thirty-nine with a decade of experience.
I could run a **training business** for the new systems, or be the mechanic everyone calls.
do: Do the **trainer qualification** first, then grow weekend teaching.
Keep trunking while the **pay is good**.
Save for a **flat deposit** before things shift.
feel: He feels **calm**, with some **excitement** about what he might build.
S4.quote: Ten years is a whole career for some people. Newer drivers should stop pretending it won't happen and pick something to learn.
fieldNote: With a decade, his plans shift from **escape to building** a business.
He sets a clear **tripwire**: if hubs stop hiring early, he moves faster.
His sense of fairness shows in wanting to **teach older drivers** too.

steps.text: Grow weekend driver teaching into a small training business
Keep trunking full time while the pay is good
Save for a deposit on a flat

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Not because I can't adapt, but because everyone would be adapting at once and there wouldn't be enough seats. What would help is carriers being made to train their own drivers for the new jobs, mechanic courses and operations rooms, before they bring in the driverless trucks.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask about the swap points. At midnight you meet drivers from the other direction and share a coffee. When the trucks drive themselves, that conversation just disappears, and nobody counts that.

headlineQuote: At midnight you meet drivers from the other direction and share a coffee. When the trucks drive themselves, that conversation just disappears, and nobody counts that.
portrait: Umar is a **27-year-old trunk driver** running nights between two parcel hubs, single, renting above a bakery.
He's an **everyday AI user** who sees its limits and is restless more than worried.
In the gentler scenarios he sees a **chance to climb**, through teaching and fleet software.
In the two-year AGI picture he admits his route **goes first**, and hedges on two retrains.
With a decade he plans to **build a training business** and still buy a flat.
biggestWorry: The two-year **AGI** picture, because everyone would be adapting at once with **too few seats**.
whatWouldHelp: He wants carriers **required to train** their drivers for mechanic and operations jobs before going driverless.
